chapter_theme: The close of Padumaiyar Ilampakam: Padumai's friend consoles her for Civakan's night departure, first by belittling men's love, then by teaching the tree of suffering from ignorance to death and the impermanence of youth, wealth and union, and lastly by omens; her mother reads Civakan's veiled sayings as a promise to return, and Civakan, disguised, tells the king's searchers he will be back within ten months.

cast.role: the princess whom Civakan married after curing her snakebite, and whom he leaves by night
Padumai's own mother, the king's queen (மாபெருந் தேவி)
Padumai's mothers, her mother and foster mothers
the men the king sends to find Civakan
the hero, called காளை and விடலை here, leaving Padumai in disguise

1388.reading: The friend goes on: men who clasp long-eyed women in close embrace, sinking into them like a striped tiger, still do not grieve when they part, and there are none so foolish as women who melt and lose their dignity over them.

claims.claim: men do not grieve at parting, and women who waste away over them are foolish

1388.nuance: The friend's consolation begins by belittling men's love (continuing 1387) before it turns, in 1389, to the nature of birth itself.

1389.reading: She sets out a tree of suffering: born from the seed of ignorance, it sprouts deeds as its trunks of pain, sends down desire as its root, branches into love and elation, flowers into sorrow, bears great affliction as fruit and ripens into death.

claims.claim: from ignorance come deeds, from deeds pain and desire, and from these love, sorrow, affliction and at last death

1389.nuance: The verse names no school. Its order (ignorance, then deeds, then feeling and craving, ending in death) resembles the chain of dependent arising taught in Manimekalai 30, but it is cut down to one image and put in a friend's mouth to dry a lover's tears; love (காதல்) itself is one of the branches.

1390.reading: As the path a bee has flown or a fish has swum under the rippled water leaves no trace even to those who watch unblinking, the human body passes away unseen, so she asks the doe-eyed princess whether it is fitting to waste her flesh in brooding.

claims.claim: the human body perishes without leaving a trace

1391.reading: If the tears we have wept, pining for those who left us in our former births, were gathered together, the sea would not hold them; look, she says, at how this weeping has only now taken its first step.

claims.claim: in the long round of births one has already shed more tears for parted kin than the sea holds

1391.nuance: Line 4 (பரிந்தழு வதற்குப் பாவா யடியிட்ட வாறு கண்டாய்) is read as 'see how this weeping has set its first foot'; the sense of the half-line is not secure.

1392.reading: To weep in love and be unable to bear it is easy, and easy too to let the life leave one's bones; what is hard in this world is to be crushed by sorrow and yet carry that sorrow and live as if it were joy.

claims.claim: bearing sorrow as if it were joy is harder than weeping or dying

1393.reading: Born by delusion into the human womb, parting and death are by nature what comes here in less than a blink; those who will not grant it even the span of a fish-eyed glance take worry on worry and sink in the poison sea of births of their own making.

claims.claim: parting and death belong to human birth by its very nature
those who grieve over what is natural sink deeper into the sea of births

1393.nuance: The play of மயற்கை, இயற்கை and செயற்கை (delusion, nature, what is made) carries the argument: birth comes from delusion, parting is its nature, and the drowning is self-made; the division of line 3 is doubtful.

1394.reading: Seeing old age within youth, affliction within wealth, parting from kin within union and sickness within health, she tells the princess with eyes fiercer than a spear to put away grief even for the blink of an eye.

claims.claim: every good state carries its opposite within it: youth age, wealth affliction, union parting, health disease

1395.reading: Do not grieve, she says: he will come back to your hand like a ball that has left it, for the owl that lives in the hollow calls in pairs, and the one who tasted your pearl smile has not left you.
1395.nuance: The consolation turns from doctrine to omen: the owl's paired call is read as a sign of reunion.

1396.reading: She recalls that in the grove, under the shade of the asoka, when a bird spoke of what was to come, she looked at the princess and foretold a cruel trouble from a fanged snake; she, called cruel then, does not speak falsely now, and telling her not to droop she lifts her up.
1396.event: The friend reminds Padumai that her earlier omen of the snake came true and lifts her up.
1396.nuance: கொடியனாய் பிழைப்புக் கூறேன் is read as the friend's 'I, whom you called cruel, do not speak amiss'; the earlier warning she cites is not traced here to a particular verse.

1397.reading: The friend gathers the princess's garland and hair in her hand, wipes the tears pouring from her eyes and holds her on her lap; the night ends, and with it the good woman's heart too grows dry.
1397.event: The friend dries Padumai's tears and holds her in her lap until dawn.
1397.nuance: புலர்ந்தது plays on dawn breaking and the heart drying of its tears.

1398.reading: As the string of a ripe, sweet song snaps in the middle, so the young man left her in the full ripeness of love, and the princess's mothers, their tears like clear dew, became like a lotus grove withered by frost.
1398.event: Padumai's mothers learn that Civakan has gone and are stricken.

1399.reading: Her own mother, melting and worn, asks the jasmine-haired girl whether her husband ever said anything before, and the gentle girl murmurs what he said in the night.
1399.event: Padumai's mother asks whether Civakan said anything beforehand, and Padumai repeats his night words.

1400.reading: She reports that he said it is a man's duty to think of the hot wasteland and leave for deeds and for wealth, and a woman's duty, if he goes, to stay at home with dignity.

claims.claim: going away for deeds and wealth is a man's duty, and staying at home with dignity a woman's

1400.nuance: Civakan's words, given in his voice through Padumai's report, are the akam rule for the man's leaving; but he has not gone for work or wealth, and in hindsight the rule was a hint covering a secret departure.

1401.reading: The broad-chested man, she says, also told her that though the royal swan that played on the scented lotus may rest elsewhere, it has no thought for the massed blue lilies.
1401.nuance: A second veiled saying: away from the lotus, the swan will not turn to other flowers, a promise of faithfulness disguised as a remark about birds.

1402.reading: As the girl of the gold-bearing breasts told this, she made her mother glad, as the asunam deer is gladdened on hearing the sweet voice of the lute.
1402.event: Padumai's report of his words gladdens her mother.

1403.reading: The king's great queen reads the riddle: he is the swan and you the lotus; he has left you but has not left you in love, and that is what he told you.
1403.event: Padumai's mother interprets Civakan's saying as a promise to return.

1404.reading: As a lotus bruised by falling frost regains its beauty when it meets the radiant sun, so the bangled girl, at the firm word that her husband will come, regained her beauty, and she spoke with words sweeter than honey.
1404.event: Padumai revives at the assurance that Civakan will return and speaks.

1405.reading: Poison does not become nectar because one licks it calling it nectar, and a peacock does not become Garuda though it kills a fearful snake; why then, she asks, should I, being such, wither for a deceiver?
1405.nuance: The two proverbs can be read against him (he only seemed a Garuda when he cured her snakebite) or against her own grief (calling it sweet does not make it so); the turn from revived beauty in 1404 to 'deceiver' here is abrupt, and the reading is not secure.

1406.reading: Dawn: the birds in the lotus pools sound like drums, the sun stretches out his rays as bright long hands, draws off the cover of black night, looks slowly over the adorned earth-woman and reaches the brow of the snowy mountain.

1407.reading: All that had befallen the girl of lute-sweet speech was carried to the king, and the king of horsed chariots, grieved, ordered them to search by every road and bring the man back within the blink of an eye.
1407.event: The king hears of Padumai's grief and sends men to search for Civakan.

1408.reading: Taking on a form born from within himself, as a lightning flash born inside lightning, the one bright as gold born from gold set his face to the north.
1408.event: Civakan takes on another form and heads north.
1408.nuance: தன்னுளே பிறந்ததோர் வடிவு is read as a changed shape he assumes, a disguise; how he takes it is not said here.

1409.reading: He bound on his anklets, made his white cloth into two pieces, took off the many ornaments he wore and gave them to a man, and set out on the long road, bright as the full moon.
1409.event: Civakan puts off his ornaments, gives them away, dresses in two white cloths and sets out on the long road.
1409.nuance: The putting off of ornaments and the plain white cloth look forward to renunciation, though here they are only a traveller's disguise.

1410.reading: The men the king sent meet the young man and say: you closely resemble our lord, in youth and in form this is he; if on the way you saw anyone go by in the night just past, tell us, sir, and we will catch up with him.
1410.event: The king's searchers meet the disguised Civakan and ask him about the man they seek.
1410.nuance: The irony is the scene's point: they tell the man himself that he looks like the one they seek.

1411.reading: He answers that within the limit of ten months they will see the beloved of the long-eyed girl, that this is no lie, and bids them go and tell it to the son of the king of the elephants in rut.
1411.event: Civakan, unrecognized, sends the searchers back with word that Padumai's husband will return within ten months.
1411.nuance: மைந்தனுக்கு (to the son) is unexpected, since the king himself sent them; it may name the king by his lineage or a prince of the house.

links.note: The Manimekalai's teacher sets out the forward chain from contact to craving, clinging, becoming and a birth whose fruit is aging, death and grief; the friend's tree runs from the seed of ignorance through deeds and desire to the fruit of death.
links.teaches: The two epics share the shape of a causal chain from ignorance to death, but the Cintamani makes it a single growing tree with love and elation among its branches and uses it to dry a lover's tears, where the Manimekalai gives it as a doctrine of release with named links.

links.note: The Kural calls craving the seed that yields unceasing birth; the friend's tree has ignorance as its seed and desire as its root.
links.teaches: Put beside the couplet, the verse shows a different order of causes: craving is not the first cause but what anchors the tree once ignorance has sown it, so cutting desire alone would not uproot it.

gains.a: a known single-cause maxim against which its own order of seed and root stands out
gains.b: an account of what lies behind craving, which the couplet leaves unasked

links.note: The Kural promises distinction to one who takes what hurts as pleasure; the friend says that bearing sorrow as joy is harder than weeping or dying.
links.teaches: The couplet's discipline for a man in adversity becomes, in a deserted bride's chamber, the hardest thing in the world, set above death itself in difficulty, so the epic measures the cost the couplet only rewards.

gains.a: a recognized rule of endurance, which shows its consolation to be ethical counsel and not just comfort
gains.b: a test case in grief over a loved one, where the rule is admitted to be harder than dying

links.note: Naladiyar 23 has wedding drums turn into funeral drums in the same hall the same day; the friend sees parting within union, age within youth and sickness within health.
links.teaches: The quatrain shows one reversal as an event; the verse turns it into a rule that every good state already holds its opposite, and uses that rule to forbid even a blink of grief.

gains.a: a concrete scene of union turned into loss that grounds its abstract list
gains.b: a generalization of its single reversal into four, with parting from kin named among them

links.note: In 1360 Civakan slips from Padumai's sleeping arms in the dark like a good life leaving the body; here the friend teaches that parting and death both belong by nature to human birth.
links.teaches: The narrator's simile of departure as death is taken up as doctrine: the parting that was likened to the soul's leaving is now said to be of the same kind as death, and as little to be grieved.

links.note: The friend says she once foretold a cruel trouble from a fanged snake; 1271 tells how a snake living in the grove bit the princess.
links.teaches: Her old warning, proved by the snakebite that brought Civakan to Padumai, is what gives her new omen of his return its weight.

links.note: The friend reads the owl's paired call as a sign that he has not left her; Civakan, unrecognized, sends word that her beloved will be seen within ten months.
links.teaches: The omen is confirmed out of the absent man's own mouth, and given a term, so the chapter closes the friend's consolation with the hero's pledge.

links.note: Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves her for wealth across the waste, then wealth alone is wealth and grace exists nowhere; Civakan's saying makes leaving for deeds and wealth a man's duty and staying a woman's.
links.teaches: The Sangam woman's voice hears the man's going for wealth as the end of grace, while the epic puts the same convention in the hero's mouth as a duty, and uses it, untruly, to cover a departure that is neither for work nor for wealth.

gains.a: the akam convention it quotes, with the woman's protest that the hero's maxim leaves out
gains.b: the man's own statement of the rule as duty, which the woman's lament answers

new_concepts.gloss: an omen read from the body or from creatures (sneezing, a throbbing eye, a lizard's chirp, an owl's cry) as a sign of the absent lover's thought or return
new_concepts.label_source: id as used in the Kainnilai marks; the word is not in these verses, which read an owl's paired call (1395) and a bird's foretelling (1396)

source_issues: Most verses were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build (FLAG repaired); word division inside joined lines is often doubtful.
1391 line 4 and 1393 line 3 are hard to divide and construe.
1411 line 4 மைந்தனுக்கு (to the king's son) sits oddly with 1407, where the king himself sends the searchers.
